title: 'We feel the pain': Pochettino on 4-0 defeat at Liverpool to start Manchester United era – video
text:
Liverpool thrashed 10-man Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday to climb to fourth in the Premier League. But the defeat left United 19th, only one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace. There was no new manager bounce for Mauricio Pochettino, who saw Leny Yoro sent off in the eighth minute for a last-ditch foul on Alexander Isak.

Pochettino accepted full responsibility for the loss, but claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. 'It was a desperate take,"' writes Andy Hunter at Anfield.

title: ‘It’s painful for me’: Pochettino criticises Yoro red card in Anfield humiliation
author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
text:
Manchester United lose 4-0 to Liverpool after early red

Argentinian suffers club’s joint-heaviest debut defeat

Mauricio Pochettino argued that Leny Yoro was wrongly sent off and that Manchester United were earlier denied a penalty against Liverpool after suffering the joint-heaviest debut defeat in the club’s history.

Liverpool’s emphatic 4-0 win ensured Pochettino equalled Lal Hilditch’s unwanted record from 1926 of losing his first United game by such a scoreline. United’s 34 goals conceded across all competitions this season are the most by any team in European football’s top five leagues.

United were reduced to 10 men after only eight minutes when Yoro was shown a straight red card for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. “He was clearly the last man and it was clearly a foul,” said the Liverpool head coach, Andoni Iraola.

Yet Pochettino took a fiercely opposing view, claiming Isak had waited for contact to be made after losing possession and insisting United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. Dominik Szoboszlai opened the scoring from the free-kick that resulted from Yoro’s foul and Liverpool were coasting at 2-0 after only 14 minutes. United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree [it was a red-card offence]because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control.

“Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul. But two minutes before, Jacquet and Mbeumo, how can you compare the situation?

“It is painful for me and for them but we played for more than 80 minutes at Anfield with 10 men. You can be critical of the team, but it’s a penalty for Mbeumo. We can make a mistake and we were punished. They can make a mistake and they were not punished.”

Pochettino defended his decision to give Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 12 months despite the centre-back having a torrid time against Liverpool’s forward line. He also claimed United showed the resolve necessary to drag themselves out of relegation trouble despite being comprehensively outplayed.

“We need to accept the reality and we need to be united,” he said. “It is clear what happened.

“After eight minutes the plan was in the bin, but what I learned from my players is that they like to fight, they are committed to the team, to the club and they want to win games.

“Today was a test that for me is very positive. Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more. We are in a situation that is very complicated and difficult, but we fight, we make the effort.”

Rio Ngumoha became the youngest goalscorer in the fixture’s Premier League history and produced a scintillating display alongside the equally impressive Florian Wirtz. Iraola said of the teenager: “He is playing a lot of minutes, on the left and the right, and he is getting used to going outside or cutting inside to finish. I’m happy with the way he arrived in the box to score. The same with Flo. We want them to be more of a threat in the box.”

Iraola recreated Jürgen Klopp’s post-match celebration after the final whistle and fist-pumped the Kop. He said: “Obviously I enjoyed the moment. I still think we owe the fans because they have been very supportive and we’ve had much better results away from home than at home. This is a big game for everyone in the club and we wanted to give them a big win.”

title: Pochettino’s new-manager bounce falls flat with De Ligt move a disastrous step | Jamie Jackson
author: Jamie Jackson at Anfield
text:
Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit

Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino .

This ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

He is firmly in the dock for this loss, due to a disastrous preference for Matthijs de Ligt over Harry Maguire, the hapless Dutch defender playing a leading part in three Liverpool goals.

Towards the end the Kop chirped: “You’re going down with the City.” There may be truth in the humour unless Pochettino gets hold – fast – of the rabble inherited from Michael Carrick .

Eight short minutes into a nascent tenure and a disgusted shake of his flowing locks was the greeting to the madhouse he has taken over. By then Leny Yoro had been sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak and Anfield was in bearpit mood.

Very far from ideal – and worse was to follow. Far worse. After the Frenchman departed, Dominik Szoboszlai smashed the free-kick through a nonexistent wall and beyond Senne Lammens and Liverpool were 1-0 up.

The visitors’ next act? To enter full meltdown as Diogo Dalot allowed Rio Ngumoha room to cross and Florian Wirtz hooked home, De Ligt losing his man.

Thirteen minutes in and 2–0 behind made Omar Berrada’s talk of the “buzz” of Pochettino’s entrance at United farcical and made the chief executive appear to be as much as a chump as his latest appointee, who was authoring a new head-coach plummet, not bounce.

Yoro had been forced into hauling down Isak after De Ligt lost first the ball, then the Liverpool striker. De Ligt’s inclusion was Pochettino’s headline selection move, the dropping of Maguire handing the centre-back a first league start in a year and it backfired almost immediately.

“I don’t know who played the last game – we assessed the squad from the day we arrived and we believe it’s the best team for today,” Pochettino said beforehand when quizzed about the XI he sent out.

Words to haunt him and, as De Ligt’s only other start was in United’s 4-1 humiliation at Como last month in the Champions League, questions regarding the coach’s judgment were already being posed.

By now “sacked in the morning” was the derisory cry of Kopites as Pochettino’s new project was in the damage-limitation mode of a 5-3-1 with 21 minutes played, as off went Bryan Mbeumo for Maguire.

After spells with Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA, Pochettino’s honours roll reads one Ligue 1 and one Coupe de France – a modest two trophies in a 17-year managerial career.

Losing a Champions League final (with Spurs) and two EFL Cup finals (Spurs and Chelsea) had characterised him, to some, as a “bridesmaid” and at half‑time his team were definitively second best, fortunate to be only two behind.

In the perpetual soap opera that is United, the buildup featured a drone filming Pochettino’s first training session, Berrada’s interview and Bruno Fernandes saying new contract talks between the captain and club were paused due to the worst league start in 40 years.

Going into the game, United’s dire form contained a solitary win in 10 league matches and eight points. Why? Because they are a rabble, lacking cohesion from goalkeeper to attack, with individuals consistently embarrassing themselves and the shirt.

It cost Carrick, culpable for this too, his job and cleared the path for Pochettino to occupy a role he has long coveted. Each new manager since Ferguson has faced a two-pronged challenge: the state of the squad and the state of the club – each related.

Those who know Pochettino say he will bring charm and warmth – useful, maybe, for man-managing a group of multimillionaires, but at the interval he needed to perform the miracle of convincing them that something, somehow, could be salvaged after a diabolical opening 45 minutes.

They were staring at defeat by an Andoni Iraola side that began 10 points and 15 places better off. Pochettino hoped to avoid this by taking off Matheus Cunha for Joshua Zirkzee for the second half but ended the non-contest ashen‑faced, with Berrada and Jason Wilcox, the director of football, appearing just as lost in the posh seats.

A main takeaway from Berrada’s interview was his conviction that “we are heading in the right direction”. When he spoke United were 18th, and by full time they were 19th, with De Ligt a glaring emblem of their disarray. When again he was marking air not Isak, the Swede saved the centre-back more blushes by spraying wide.

This had Pochettino applauding, unfathomably, when invective seemed an apt response.

Yet when Ngumoha made it 3-0 after 66 minutes there was no more faux touchline enthusiasm from a man who had promised to “create something from scratch”. As with all who have followed Ferguson, he had discovered that United’s shaky foundations make building anything sustainable a sisyphean task.

De Ligt’s loose pass led to Víctor Muñoz’s fourth, meaning the answer to whether Pochettino’s debut could have gone any worse was a resounding no.

title: Camara to continue with Haas for final two races
text:
Brazilian Rafael Camara will continue to race for the Haas team for the final two grands prix of the Formula 1 season.

The 21-year-old, who was already signed to drive for the US-based team in 2027 , was drafted in for this month's Sao Paulo Grand Prix after Frenchman Esteban Ocon was dropped following a bust-up with team boss Ayao Komatsu.

The decision to keep Camara in the Haas seat in preparation for next season means he will likely lose the Formula 2 title.

He is leading the F2 championship by seven points from Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov heading into the final two events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Komatsu said: "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and build on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America.

"I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team.

"We now get to finish the season together which is advantageous to us all ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get under way."

A statement from Haas announcing the move did not include a quote from Camara.

title: Liverpool hand Pochettino nightmare Manchester United start after Yoro sees red
author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
text:
Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United . On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino endured a baptism of fire from the eighth minute onwards when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else while tormenting their old rivals yet again.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz. Liverpool’s two creative forces were also on the scoresheet as Ngumoha became the youngster scorer in the fixture’s Premier League history.

“Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic game in the job. There may well be more. On this evidence, 19th in the Premier League is not a misleading reflection of United’s position.

The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who met his new charges only on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how quickly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage-limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first big call in the job proved a serious mistake with destructive repercussions for United’s entire evening.

That ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia, but his replacement at centre-back was heavily responsible for the chaos that quickly unfolded. The Netherlands international was at fault for three goals. Liverpool , under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the first mishap in the visitors’ central defence.

De Ligt lost the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee, Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save Yoro. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.

Pochettino claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. It was a desperate take. A simple detail showed the extent of the job United’s latest head coach has on his hands: the wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the isolated exception of Bruno Fernandes, no one covered the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.

Liverpool devoured the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.

The first chants of “sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was, of course, a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.

Pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead.

Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from his fellow £100m+ recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery by Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before delivering an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert.

Iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the midweek Champions League trip to Club Brugge and he started resting players from the 72nd minute onwards. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, was pounced on by Wirtz who released Muñoz inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do up in the directors’ box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend the actor James Nesbit. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

title: Fernandes puts contract talks on hold; Liverpool v Manchester United buildup and more – matchday live
author: Dominic Booth (now) Emillia Hawkins (earlier)
text:
Bruno Fernandes has revealed that he put contract talks with Manchester United on hold after being offered a new deal.

Speaking to Sky Sports ahead of the match against Liverpool, the United captain explained: “No, there’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that he’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here. I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here. The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.

“Yeah, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And as you said, there are no negotiations going on.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season, we came in the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations because the most important thing now is that the club gets back to win games.”

Fernandes’ current deal expires at the end of the season, but Manchester United have the option to extend it by another year.

title: Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'
text:
Warning: This article contains offensive language

Max Verstappen was a constant amid the chaos at a remarkable Las Vegas Grand Prix.

He was the star figure in a race that had 34 overtaking moves for the lead in 50 laps and 352 overall, in which the biggest advantage the leader ever had was 1.5 seconds, and in which there were five cars fighting nose to tail for the lead to the final lap, and for much of the race many more than that.

Even better for Verstappen, George Russell made a critical mistake 24 hours after he had revived his long-standing, on-off spat with the Dutchman.

Russell, who had been Verstappen's main threat from the start of the race, locked up his brakes and speared into the barrier trying to pass Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli for second place behind Verstappen with two laps to go.

Verstappen said: "He speaks a lot next to the track, and it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, you know?

"And today, karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening. I was, like, "Fantastic, my day is only getting better."

"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Verstappen felt motivated to make these remarks because of what Russell had said the day before.

After an on-track altercation in practice, the pair had had an exchange of views in the stewards' room. Then, after Verstappen took pole from Russell - after fastest man Antonelli's five-place penalty was taken into account - the Briton took a pop at the Dutchman.

"I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else," Russell said. "Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

In the paddock, a number of people felt that Verstappen was probably not the right "guy" to pick a fight with.

Even though Russell was battling with Verstappen throughout the race, the nature of their drives was different.

Russell would pass the Red Bull on the straight. Then Verstappen would reclaim the lead in more extreme fashion, on the outside of the fast kink leading on to the pit straight, or on the outside again at the long Turn Three.

Hardly anyone else even tried these moves, let alone pulled them off. Verstappen made them look routine.

After his error, Russell managed to extricate himself from the crash barrier, but he had turned a certain podium finish into a ninth place.

It was the perfect encapsulation of a season in which almost nothing has gone right.

For Verstappen, it was almost too good to be true.

The race was unlike any grand prix anyone younger than about 70 had ever seen.

The fabled slipstreaming battles of a pre-chicane Monza in the 1960s and early 1970s - that led to the closest ever finish in F1 history at the 1971 Italian Grand Prix, , external when the first five cars crossed the line 0.6secs apart - were the closest comparison at the highest echelon of the sport.

In modern terms, it was more reminiscent of American oval racing, where the high-speed nature of the race tracks leads to long chains of cars slipstreaming and lots of overtaking, little of it meaningful until the final stages.

Mercedes F1 team boss Toto Wolff pretty much hit the nail on the head when he said: "It was Indy 500 and Nascar and Formula 1 mixed - I enjoyed it."

And it encapsulated something else about F1 2026 - the internal debate that has been raging in the sport about artificiality ever since the latest engines were introduced.

The near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power has created energy-starved cars where the batteries run out before the end of long straights.

On certain tracks this has led to a form of racing known as "yo-yo", where cars constantly pass and re-pass each other depending on their respective levels of battery charge.

After a chaotic few races early in the year, this has diminished as teams have better understood energy management.

But in Las Vegas the combination of long straights and slipstreaming brought it to its apotheosis. And no-one quite knew what to think about it.

Verstappen said: "Really, really surreal and something that I've never seen before in Formula 1 myself.

"It was just a crazy amount of fighting. The slipstream was so big that you - it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were just following you.

"It was just very exciting, I guess, for everyone to watch. I know, of course, it's a big show around here the whole weekend, and I hope that we delivered on track."

That was a carefully judged answer for the television cameras, the sort that sounds like one thing, but if you know the person's real views, you can read between the lines to see the nuances that hint at something else.

In the news conference, Verstappen's true feelings came out. Was it a kind of racing he enjoyed?

"When I look at it from my racer heart, not," he said. "When you look at it as a show spectacle, yes.

"I enjoyed my repassing and everything, but I prefer to look at it with my racing heart. Even my heart rate, I was not nervous at all because it's just felt kind of cruising out there, just trying to press the battery whenever it was correct or defend.

"But for the show, when you look at it from the outside, probably, yes, you like it. But, yeah, I don't know.

"I probably shouldn't say it. I probably should not. I remember winning one like this when I was playing Mario Kart.

"Sometimes you drop back and you get drafts, and there's like a catch-up, you know? Always when you're dropping back, you go faster. So that's the last time that I felt something like this."

title: Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.

The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.

And in the final laps Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli, and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.

The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.

And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.

Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.

It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines this year.

But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.

The key stories of an engrossing race were:

Verstappen's remarkable intelligence and control in the lead in the most demanding of circumstances

Another dip in a dreadful season for Russell

More controversy at Ferrari, as both drivers earned 10-second penalties for driving infringements in battles involving the other

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Andrew Benson Q&A: Send us your questions

"How many overtakes did I do?" Verstappen asked his engineer on the slowing down lap, as he reflected on a race the like of which F1 has not seen since the famous Monza slipstreaming battles of the 1960s and early 1970s.

"Yeah, and not many of them on the straight," his new engineer Tom Hart said, summing up how Verstappen had secured the win against the Mercedes challenge.

Lap after lap after lap, Verstappen, who started from pole, would lose the lead to Russell on the Strip only to reclaim it at the last corner, usually going around the outside.

If that did not work, and Russell passed later in the lap, or led across the line, Verstappen developed a trademark move around the outside of Turn Three to get back in front.

The race went on and on like that, punctuated by a mid-grand prix safety car, but through it all Verstappen always seemed in control.

As the race wore on, Antonelli came into the picture after starting sixth, and passed Russell with 12 laps to go to become Verstappen's main challenger.

Now it was the Italian's turn to swap places with Verstappen, but again the Dutchman had the measure of Mercedes.

At one point, Verstappen asked his team to come up with a better deployment strategy for the final lap because he thought Mercedes had "figured it out".

They came back to him to say that he had already come up with the best approach.

In the end, though, he need not have worried, as his rivals behind him gave him enough of a gap at the start of the final lap to not have to worry too much about defending his lead.

That critical final phase started with Russell deciding to make a move to become Verstappen's challenger again.

Russell went for a move into Turn Five with two laps to go but he locked up his brakes over the bumps heading into the corner - bumps that had earlier taken Red Bull's Isack Hadjar out of the lead battle when his front wing broke over them - and went straight on into the barrier.

Russell managed to reverse out of the barrier, but a ninth-place finish was not what he was expecting.

The incident was also unfortunate for him in the context of his calling out Verstappen's driving after qualifying, when he said "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

Verstappen had the last word, both on track and literally. After seeing Russell's embarrassing mistake, Verstappen came on the radio to say: "Hah, hah. Well done. My God."

Now Antonelli looked to be the man who would challenge Verstappen for the win.

But that was counting without the McLarens. Piastri had already driven an outstanding race to recover from starting 17th because of an engine penalty and Norris had at one point dropped out of the top 10 in the chaotic lead battle in the first part of the grand prix.

But they were third and fourth around the penultimate lap and in what looked like a co-ordinated attack but certainly wasn't, both swept around Antonelli around the outside of the fast final corner heading into the last lap.

That gave Verstappen breathing space, and Antonelli was delayed sufficiently that he could not recover to challenge them.

Second-placed Norris summed it up, saying: "I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1. I didn't know what was happening half the time."

A hectic end to the season means Formula 1 moves from Las Vegas to the Middle East next weekend, for the Qatar Grand Prix at the Lusail International Circuit from 27-29 November.

title: Verstappen's superb racecraft & Russell's costly mistake - driver ratings
text:
Max Verstappen sealed his fourth win of the season with a stunning victory at a chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver fought off his rivals for the lead throughout the race and crossed the line ahead of the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

George Russell, who started second, locked up late on attempting a move on Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli and finished ninth, while Charles Leclerc was given a 10-second time penalty for making contact with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Vegas.

A superb display of racecraft. Inherited pole after Kimi Antonelli's grid penalty and spent virtually the entire race being attacked, passed and then finding a way back through, while also working out the optimum energy deployment from inside his Red Bull. One of his finest victories.

A remarkable recovery after dropping as low as 11th in the madness of the opening part of the race. Had genuine pace throughout and fought all the way back to second, finishing less than a second behind Verstappen.

One of the drives of the race. Qualified seventh but started 17th because of his engine penalty and charged all the way through to the podium, gaining 14 places and joining McLaren team-mate Norris in passing Antonelli right at the end.

Fastest of everyone in qualifying and a genuine contender for victory despite starting sixth because of his engine penalty. Battled Verstappen superbly before his Mercedes' energy deployment problem on the final lap cost him two places, although he still recovered fourth from Pierre Gasly before the flag.

An excellent weekend and comfortably Alpine's best result of the season. Reached Q3, stayed with the leading group throughout and was less than three seconds away from victory at the finish.

Another huge result for Alpine. Qualified inside the top 10, stayed out of trouble while plenty around him didn't and converted ninth on the grid into sixth place.

A messy weekend but there was still plenty of fight in the race. Missing Q3 was disappointing and the 10-second time penalty for passing Norris off the circuit was harsh, although being spun by Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc later on was not his fault and he recovered to finish seventh.

A superb recovery from 20th on the grid after his power-unit penalty. Kept himself in contention throughout, made up 12 places and even pinched eighth from Russell at the line to secure Williams' joint-best result of the season.

For 48 laps this was heading towards a very high score. Fastest in both second and final practice, qualified third and spent most of the race going toe-to-toe with Verstappen for the lead. But locking up and putting it into the barrier with two laps remaining was an enormous and costly mistake.

A frustrating weekend from start to finish. Ferrari's qualifying struggles left him 11th and although he recovered well enough to finish sixth on the road, spinning his team-mate Hamilton earned a 10-second time penalty and dropped him to 10th.

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

A solid weekend without quite finding the points. Led Audi in qualifying and again in the race, eventually finishing 11th after spending much of the evening embroiled in the midfield fight.

Similar story to team-mate Hulkenberg but just a little further back. Started 13th, finished 12th and narrowly held off Haas' Oliver Bearman at the flag.

A very good recovery after starting last because of power-unit penalties. Climbed nine positions, raced aggressively with both Audis and finished only two-tenths behind Bortoleto.

Qualified eighth and had looked set for another strong result before a fuel leak forced him to start from the pit lane. Recovering to 15th after effectively beginning the race out of contention was a decent salvage job.

The final position tells almost none of the story. Qualified fifth, started fourth and was part of the lead fight until his Red Bull front wing failed over the bumps after the safety-car restart. The pace was there for a huge result. He lost a position after the race because of a 10-second penalty for driving slowly and holding up Russell before they pitted under the safety car.

Another respectable showing in only his second grand prix for Haas. Narrowly missed Q2 and was running steadily before being spun in the Sergio Perez collision, then recovered from the back after the safety car to finish 16th.

Another difficult weekend for Aston Martin. Qualified 20th before his engine penalty pushed him further back and there was little progress to be made during the race.

Qualified at the back and Cadillac again lacked the pace to threaten the midfield. At least he stayed in the fight with the Aston Martins and made it to the finish after several recent retirements.

Aston Martin simply never looked competitive. Qualified 19th, spent the race towards the back and retired late on.

A real missed opportunity for the Briton and his Racing Bulls team. Sixth in qualifying and fifth on the grid was superb, and he was still right in the leading train when the safety car came out. Spinning while trying to warm the tyres behind it and eventually retiring was a costly unforced error.

Qualified only 18th but appeared to have better race pace and was making progress before the collision with Camara ended his afternoon.

A weekend that ended before the race even started. Qualified 16th and was due to start 14th, but overheating rear brakes on the laps to the grid caused enough damage to prevent Williams from racing the car.

title: Hamilton-Leclerc collision completely unacceptable, says Ferrari boss
text:
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc face yet another tense discussion over their ability to race together cleanly on track after colliding in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc tipped Hamilton into a spin with 22 laps to go, costing both points in a race where at one stage they were racing with the McLarens, which finished on the podium.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, which meant he finished 10th, three places behind Hamilton, in a race won by Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

It was the second race-compromising incident within grands prix, and it came after the drivers had been brought together to clear the air at the last race in Brazil after their first-lap fighting in Mexico cost them a win.

Hamilton said such an incident "should never happen" but added that: "The question should be for Ferrari now."

Leclerc said: "We just need to fix whatever is not working."

Team principal Frederic Vasseur described the situation as "completely unacceptable".

Verstappen wins extraordinary race as Ferraris collide

The Frenchman said: "It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsor, the same speech as after Mexico.

"We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you're passed by others. It means you have to do your race and Charles clearly made a mistake.

"It's penalising the team a lot and it's completely unacceptable. Honestly we are more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico, we had a chat together in Brazil, today we passed the message to think about the team when racing together and the outcome is this one."

The battle between the two drivers has been tense all season, and in the second part of the year there have been a series of flashpoints, whether it be on-track racing, disputes about how best to work through strategy, and Hamilton ignoring two separate calls to pit in different races, both of which compromised his result, because he was looking at beating Leclerc.

Hamilton said: "It's not something I want to really get into."

The seven-time champion, who struggled against Leclerc last year but who has been revived in 2026, deflected questions about whether he should be given number-one status.

"I've never asked to be number one," he said. "I genuinely haven't ever asked.

"There was a point in the season where I was 40-odd points ahead, and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi (Antonelli).

"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year.

"At that point, we needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few instances in the season where, with the support, I think we could have beaten Kimi.

"But no, that's not what I've asked for. We shouldn't have gotten together. That should just never happen. But I've said everything I can on it, and the question should be for Ferrari now."

Before the incident, the drivers expressed their differing views on team radio, Leclerc expressing his concern for the way Hamilton was defending, Hamilton saying they should be focused on catching the cars in front.

Leclerc said: "He needs to be careful with this squeezing because it's not going to end well."

Hamilton swore as he asked the team to tell Leclerc to "back off", adding: "I'm trying to catch these guys ahead."

This was similar to their different stances in Mexico, when Leclerc was attacking Hamilton on the first lap while the Briton felt they should be working together to defend their one-two positions.

Vasseur said he would talk to the drivers the day after the race, once the immediate heat of the situation had dissipated.

"You can't imagine the frustration for me, but more important for the guys at home," Vasseur said.

"I want to have a discussion tomorrow. Also, Charles to digest the situation. It's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race."

Leclerc said: "I don't think it's going to be intense. None of our discussions were intense, but surely it cannot continue like that.

"I've taken a penalty, so I guess the blame is on me from the stewards and I guess from the majority, so as a result I guess it was deserved."
